title: AI Fluency for students
author: Anthropic, with Prof. Joseph Feller (University College Cork) and Prof. Rick Dakan (Ringling College)
summary: Anthropic's own short course that applies its 4D AI Fluency framework to student life: using AI as a learning partner, using it for career planning, and staying the human in the loop. Free, self-paced, with a certificate at the end.
who_for: A student who has never used Claude seriously and wants the official framing of what good AI use looks like before touching an assignment.
skip_if: You want click-by-click Claude instructions. This is a way of thinking, not a feature tutorial, and it never shows you the actual Claude interface.
notes: The course page says it assumes you already did the core 4D AI Fluency Framework course, so start there. Needs a separate Skilljar account, not your Claude account. No publication date is shown anywhere on the page. A Coursera version of the same course also exists.

title: Use Claude for Education at your university
author: Anthropic Help Center
summary: The official help page for students on a university-provided Claude account: what the education plan gives you (bigger context window, Projects, higher limits), a long list of study tasks Claude can help with, how to sign in on each device, and what to do when login or usage limits break.
who_for: A student whose university just switched on Claude for Education and who wants one page that says what they now have and how to log in.
skip_if: Your university does not provide Claude. Most of this page is about the institutional plan and will not match a personal free or Pro account.
notes: One line on academic integrity, and it is only one line: follow your university's policy. Do not treat this page as integrity guidance. No date shown, so freshness is unknowable.

title: Anthropic Education Report: How University Students Use Claude
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's analysis of a million anonymised student conversations, showing what students actually ask Claude for, how uneven adoption is between STEM and humanities, and where the company itself worries that students are handing over their thinking.
who_for: A student who wants an honest picture of how their peers use AI, and a reason to check whether their own habits are learning or outsourcing.
skip_if: You want practical instructions. This is a research write-up with charts, not a how-to, and it teaches you nothing about operating Claude.
notes: Over 12 months old and possibly outdated: the data predates Learning Mode going general, Projects templates, Skills and Cowork. Treat the numbers as historical.

title: Advancing Claude for Education
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's announcement of the education integrations that matter most to students: Canvas LTI so Claude runs inside your course, and Panopto and Wiley MCP connectors so Claude can read your lecture transcripts and your library's peer-reviewed content instead of the open web.
who_for: A student at a Claude for Education university who wants to know whether their lectures and library are connectable, and what the privacy position is.
skip_if: You use a personal Claude account. None of these integrations are available to you, and the rest of the post is university partnership news.
notes: Over 12 months old and possibly outdated. Written as a 'first look' at features 'rolling out over the next few weeks', so check with your own university what actually shipped. Useful line: conversations are private by default and excluded from training by default.

title: Claude Campus Program
author: Anthropic
summary: The page describing Claude Builder Clubs and Campus Ambassadors: student-run AI communities on campus with Anthropic speakers, hackathons, API credits and a paid stipend for club leads.
who_for: A student who wants to learn Claude by running workshops and hackathons with other students rather than by reading guides alone, in any subject, not only computer science.
skip_if: You want to learn Claude for your own coursework this week. This is a community programme, not teaching material, and it costs real organising time.
notes: Applications for the Spring 2026 cohort are closed and the page says to wait for future news, so right now this is information only. No date on the page.

title: Claude for higher education
author: Anthropic
summary: Anthropic's product page for Claude for Education, listing the student-facing pieces (Learning Mode, Study, Career and Research project templates) and which universities are partners.
who_for: A student checking whether their institution is covered and what an education account includes before asking IT for access.
skip_if: You already have access, or you want to be taught something. This is a sales page and it teaches nothing about using Claude well.
notes: Marketing page, so expect optimistic framing about academic integrity. No date, and the partner list changes without notice.

title: Using Claude Learning Mode to Study
author: Muhammad Salman, MS student, Northeastern University (CATLR AI Student Guides)
summary: A student-written explanation of when to use plain Claude chat, a Project, or Learning Mode, with a worked Calculus II example. The best part is the section on how to phrase questions so Socratic mode helps you: share your partial reasoning instead of asking for the answer.
who_for: Any student, in any subject, who wants AI that questions them instead of finishing their homework, and who needs to be shown how to talk to it.
skip_if: You want a fast answer to a specific problem. Learning Mode is deliberately slower, and this guide will annoy you if you are on a deadline tonight.
notes: Over 12 months old: the click path and screenshots show the mid-2025 Projects screen and no longer match Claude exactly. The retention and university-outcome claims are cited loosely and should not be treated as established evidence. Method still holds.

title: AI-Powered Flashcards with Claude Projects
author: Northeastern University CATLR, AI Student Guides (student-authored)
summary: Step-by-step build of a Claude Project whose knowledge base is your own lecture notes, plus a copy-paste Project Instructions prompt that makes it generate flashcards testing reasoning rather than definitions. Shows worked examples from computer science and law.
who_for: A student with slides and notes as PDFs who wants revision cards grounded in what their lecturer actually taught, not generic internet knowledge.
skip_if: You have no course files to upload, or you revise better by making cards yourself. Card-making is itself retrieval practice, and this hands that step to a machine.
notes: Recent and current. Written for a Northeastern-provided Claude account; the free tier has smaller upload limits, so a whole semester of slides may not fit.

title: How to Use AI to Help You Prepare for Quizzes and Exams
author: Northeastern University CATLR, AI Student Guides (student-authored)
summary: Two full copy-paste prompts written by a student who uses them: a Quizzer that runs an escalating self-test and adapts difficulty from your answers, and an Examiner that simulates a scored oral exam. Both work better when you upload your real course material first.
who_for: A student with an exam coming who wants active retrieval practice and pressure rehearsal instead of re-reading notes.
skip_if: You have not studied the material yet. These prompts test you, they do not teach you, and going in cold just produces a demoralising transcript.
notes: Over 12 months old and possibly outdated in its interface references, but the prompts are plain text and still work. Grades Claude first and lists ChatGPT as an alternative.

title: How to Set Up a Claude Project that Answers Questions about Your Class
author: Northeastern University CATLR, AI Student Guides (student-authored)
summary: A walkthrough of building a per-course Claude Project loaded with your syllabus, slides and readings, so Claude answers using your module rather than the internet.
who_for: A student taking one dense course who keeps re-pasting the same context into every chat and wants to stop.
skip_if: Your course materials are locked in a VLE you cannot export from, or your institution forbids uploading copyrighted readings to an AI tool. Check before you upload.
notes: Over 12 months old, so the Projects screenshots will not match the current interface. I checked the page is live and read the summary and headings, not the full walkthrough.

title: Using AI for Writing Feedback
author: Northeastern University CATLR, AI Student Guides (student-authored)
summary: A short student guide on asking AI for criticism of your own draft rather than a rewrite, so the words stay yours.
who_for: A student who has finished a draft and has nobody to read it before the deadline.
skip_if: You have access to a writing centre or a tutor. Human feedback on argument and discipline conventions is still better, and free at most universities.
notes: Over 12 months old. Short page. I confirmed it is live and read the abstract and headings only. It does not tell you to disclose the feedback step, so pair it with your institution's disclosure rules.

title: Claude for Education Is Made for Learning
author: Pitt Digital, University of Pittsburgh
summary: The clearest short onboarding page I found: a three-step vague-to-specific prompt example for an essay, the exact click path to turn on Learning Mode, when to use a Project versus a plain chat, and what Artifacts actually give you. It also tells you plainly that Claude can sound confident and be wrong.
who_for: A student, in any subject, opening Claude for the first time who wants twenty minutes that cover prompting, Learning Mode, Projects and hallucination in one place.
skip_if: You already build Projects and write structured prompts. Nothing here goes past the basics, and the Pitt login references will not apply to you.
notes: The style list (Learning, Formal, Explanatory, Concise, Normal) and the Search-and-tools click path were accurate as of December 2025; verify against your own screen. Written when Pitt student access was still 'coming soon'.

title: Claude for Education at Northumbria
author: Northumbria University IT Services
summary: A student induction page with an unusually honest section titled 'What Claude for Education won't do': it will not write your assignments, will not hand you answers to copy, and cannot reach your library's paywalled databases.
who_for: A student who wants the expectations set straight in five minutes, especially the limits, before their first assignment.
skip_if: You want technique. There are no prompts and no worked examples, and the access instructions are Northumbria-only.
notes: No date anywhere on the page, so freshness cannot be checked. The claim that Claude 'promotes good academic practice' is institutional optimism, not a guarantee.

title: Claude Enterprise at Syracuse University
author: Syracuse University Information Technology Services
summary: A campus landing page that mixes access instructions with a compact prompting primer: the Who / What / Why / How context checklist, asking Claude to think step by step, and refining through conversation rather than rewriting the prompt.
who_for: A student who wants the prompting fundamentals in one screen, plus links to Projects guides and workshop recordings.
skip_if: You are not at Syracuse. Half the links go to internal wikis and sign-up forms you cannot open.
notes: No date shown. The prompting examples are work-flavoured (emails, presentations) rather than coursework-flavoured. Nothing on academic integrity.

title: Introduction to Claude Projects
author: LSE Eden Centre
summary: An eight-minute screen walkthrough from LSE's teaching centre showing what a Claude Project is, how Project Instructions and the file knowledge base work, and why a Project beats a scattered pile of chats.
who_for: Someone who learns by watching a real screen rather than reading steps, and who wants a source with a university behind it instead of a YouTube tutorial channel.
skip_if: You are already comfortable with Projects, or you need student-specific coursework examples. The framing is aimed at LSE educators.
notes: About 8 minutes. Recorded December 2025, so the interface may have moved since. Small channel with low view counts, which is not a quality signal either way.

title: How to share projects in Claude
author: LSE Eden Centre
summary: A two-minute clip showing how to share a Claude Project with other people on the same organisation account, which is how a study group can revise from one shared knowledge base.
who_for: A study group or project team on an institutional Claude plan that wants one shared workspace instead of five private ones.
skip_if: You are on a personal Claude account. Sharing across an organisation is the whole point of the video and you do not have it.
notes: About 2 minutes. Check your assessment rules first: a shared Project on an assessed group task can blur who wrote what.

title: Plagiarism and Academic Integrity 101 in the Age of AI
author: Melisa Balos, Howard-Tilton Memorial Library, Tulane University
summary: A workshop companion guide that treats AI integrity as a judgment problem rather than a rule list: definitions, grey-area scenarios, policy, citation and disclosure, checklists, and a disclosure builder. It says openly that instructors are working this out in real time too.
who_for: Any student, at any university, who is genuinely unsure where the line is and wants scenarios rather than a policy PDF.
skip_if: You need your own institution's rules. The Policies tab is Tulane-specific and cannot substitute for your syllabus.
notes: Last updated 31 July 2026, so current. I read the Welcome and Disclosure Builder tabs in full and skimmed the rest, so this is previewed not fully reviewed. The librarian discloses that she used Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the page design only.

title: AI Disclosure Builder
author: Melisa Balos, Howard-Tilton Memorial Library, Tulane University
summary: An interactive tool plus five annotated model disclosure statements at minor, moderate and substantial levels of AI use, each explaining line by line why the wording works. It gives a usable test for when to disclose: would knowing this change how a reader assesses your work?
who_for: A student about to submit work who used AI somewhere in the process and does not know how to write the declaration.
skip_if: Your assignment bans AI outright. The page states plainly that disclosure does not make prohibited use acceptable.
notes: Last updated 31 July 2026. The always / good practice / not required split is a house view, not a universal rule; your department may draw the line differently. I read the guidance and examples but did not run the builder widget itself.

title: Acknowledging AI tools and technologies
author: Academic Skills, University of Melbourne
summary: The cleanest declaration template I found: name the tool, say how the output was used, state that a full prompt log is available on request. It lists the six uses that need declaring, gives three worked examples (one using Claude), and answers the awkward questions about group work, word counts, appendices and translation tools.
who_for: A student anywhere who needs a wording they can copy tonight, and who wants the difference between citing AI and declaring AI made plain.
skip_if: Your subject has its own declaration form. Melbourne says faculty formats take precedence, and so should yours.
notes: Page metadata gives 1 May 2026 as the last modification, so it is current. Melbourne-specific in places (Re:cite, subject coordinators), but the template travels.

title: Referencing AI and Acknowledging AI Use
author: University of Warwick Library
summary: Five long, realistic disclosure paragraphs covering information gathering, brainstorming and structuring, plus citation guidance for Harvard, APA 7, MLA 9, IEEE, MHRA 4, Chicago 18 and the new OSCOLA 5th edition. It then shows nine departments' actual policies side by side, which is the most useful part: they genuinely disagree with each other.
who_for: A student who wants to see how much a disclosure statement should really say, and proof that AI rules differ by department, not just by university.
skip_if: You only need a one-line acknowledgement. This is long, and the departmental section is Warwick-only.
notes: Created August 2025, last updated 30 June 2026. Several citation links go to Cite Them Right, which needs an institutional subscription. The guide itself warns that departmental policies may have changed since publication.

title: Documenting Your AI Use
author: St. Catherine University Library and Archives
summary: A compact page on the practical side of disclosure: what a statement must contain, four ways to save your prompt log so you can prove your process, and why shared chat links are unreliable evidence. Ends with current APA, MLA and Chicago 18th positions on citing generative AI.
who_for: A student who wants to protect themselves from a false accusation by keeping a defensible record of how they worked.
skip_if: You want to know whether you are allowed to use AI at all. This page assumes permission and only covers documenting it.
notes: Updated four days before I checked, so this is the freshest integrity page in this list. Good explicit warning against letting AI generate your citations. Creative Commons licensed, so your library can reuse it.

title: Disclosing the Use of AI
author: Princeton University Library
summary: Princeton's page on when and how to disclose AI use in research and scholarship, aimed slightly higher up the ladder than undergraduate coursework guides.
who_for: A final-year or postgraduate student whose work may end up in a thesis or a submitted paper, where publisher rules also apply.
skip_if: You are writing ordinary coursework. The Melbourne, Warwick or Tulane pages give you more usable templates for that.
notes: Created 2023 and last updated 16 July 2026. I confirmed it is live and read the headings, not the full page, so this is metadata-level only.

title: Using AI in university
author: UNSW Sydney, Academic Skills
summary: A student toolkit page built around a Levels of AI Assistance framework, which is a scale course convenors use to say exactly how much AI is allowed on a given assignment, from none to substantial.
who_for: A student who finds 'it depends on your course' unhelpful and wants a named scale to ask their tutor about.
skip_if: Your university does not use a levels framework. Asking your tutor 'which level is this?' will just confuse them.
notes: No publication or update date on the page. Recommends Microsoft Copilot, not Claude, as the privacy-safe option at UNSW. Read partially, so listed rather than reviewed.

title: AI for Students
author: Monash University
summary: A hub page linking Monash's student AI training: a Foundations in AI module with hands-on activities and a completion record, a credit-bearing 'AI for Everyone' unit for non-technical students, and separate guidance on assessments, referencing and graduate research.
who_for: A student who wants a structured, assessed path to AI literacy rather than a pile of blog posts, and who wants to see what a serious university-built curriculum looks like.
skip_if: You are not at Monash. The module and the unit are both behind institutional login, so all you get is the shape of the curriculum.
notes: Page metadata gives 29 June 2026. Monash provides Copilot and Gemini, not Claude, so the tool-specific advice will not transfer.

title: 2026 Student Guide to Artificial Intelligence
author: Elon University Imagining the Digital Future Center, AAC&U and The Princeton Review
summary: The third annual open-access student guide, subtitled 'Human Wisdom for the Age of AI'. This edition is about the human capabilities to protect rather than about tool features, and it ships with a free self-assessment and teacher learning modules.
who_for: A student who wants a considered, non-vendor view of what AI does to their thinking, from an academic association rather than a company.
skip_if: You need to operate Claude. There are no prompts, no screenshots and no product instructions in this guide at all.
notes: Creative Commons licensed. The guide itself is a large PDF at https://studentguidetoai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-Student-Guide-to-AI.pdf, which I confirmed downloads but did not read end to end. Earlier 2024 and 2025 editions are still on the site and are now outdated.

title: AI Student Research Guide: Prompt Engineering
author: Westmoreland County Community College Library
summary: One short page that teaches the four parts of a usable prompt (instruction, input data, context, output indicator) with academic examples, plus librarian Leo Lo's CLEAR framework: concise, logical, explicit, adaptive, reflective.
who_for: A student who has never thought about how they phrase a request and wants the smallest possible thing that will improve every prompt they write.
skip_if: You already write structured prompts. This is a single screen of fundamentals and will teach you nothing new.
notes: Last updated 6 July 2026. Generic to all chatbots, with no Claude-specific advice. One outbound link goes to the OpenAI API best-practices page, which is developer material and off-target for most students.

title: Generative AI and Academic Integrity
author: California State University, Northridge Library
summary: A short library page setting out where generative AI sits against a university's existing academic dishonesty definitions, kept current through August 2026.
who_for: A student who wants a plain restatement of the rule that unattributed AI text is treated like any other unattributed text.
skip_if: You have already read one of the fuller integrity guides here. This adds little beyond a summary and local policy links.
notes: Created February 2024, last updated 19 August 2026. I confirmed the page is live and read the headings only. Local CSUN policy links will not apply elsewhere.

title: AI feedback customized for student writers: the updated PAIRR prompts
author: Anna Mills, College of Marin, with the PAIRR project team (UC Davis)
summary: The openly published prompts from a funded research project on AI feedback for student writing, tested over a year by writing instructors, plus demonstration chatbots so you can see the kind of feedback they produce. The design goal is feedback that sends you back to a human reader, not away from one.
who_for: A student who wants feedback prompts that were actually studied rather than invented for a blog post, and who is willing to read the reasoning behind them.
skip_if: You want a one-line prompt. These are long, pedagogy-driven prompts written primarily for instructors to deploy, and adapting them takes effort.
notes: Substack, so expect subscription prompts. The prompts are tool-agnostic and were not tuned for Claude specifically. Metadata date is the last modification, 28 January 2026.

title: Peer and AI Review of Student Writing with Marit MacArthur and Anna Mills
author: Derek Bruff, Intentional Teaching podcast
summary: An interview with the two researchers behind PAIRR on combining peer review with AI feedback, covering student voice, metacognition, why prompts have to be tested, and linguistic justice for non-native English writers.
who_for: A student who wants to understand why their instructors are structuring AI use the way they are, and what the research actually shows about feedback.
skip_if: You want study techniques. This is a conversation aimed at teachers about course design, and there is nothing to do afterwards.
notes: Almost 12 months old but the argument is not tied to any product version. Audio only, transcript availability not verified. Also listed on Apple Podcasts and Spotify; this is the original publisher link.
